utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon, Witness. Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking. I am ready to perform my task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Chana, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jasarevic. We will now continue with your testimony. Before the adjournment yesterday, I was asking you about your relationship generally and the attitude of both the 9th and the 10th Brigade to military security, and in that context I asked you - and that was the last question I put to you - was: Did you know a man named Amir Deljkic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who he was, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Deljkic was a member of the 1st Corps' security service, an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what happened to him, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day early in the morning, he was on his way to work. He was ambushed in his own street by members of the 10th Mountain Brigade. They took him to their command post and mistreated him - that is perhaps the simplest way to put it - in a very brutal way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How did you get to know about this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, someone from the security service of the 1st Corps told me. The same day or some hours later - I can't remember specifically - his wife came over and complained to me, asking for help. She was crying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a bid to help Mr. Deljkic and being unable to get in touch with the commander of the 10th Brigade, since it was quite obvious that he was the only one in a position to help or release Mr. Deljkic, I went back to Mr. Sefer Halilovic, as Chief of Staff and a person I knew and valued very highly as my former superior, appealing to him to help Mr. Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why was it that you chose to go to Mr. Halilovic over this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of his command position, he was in a position of authority. Besides, he was a person I knew and trusted. It was the most natural thing for me to go to him. Commander Delic was not a person I knew well at the time; whereas, I knew Mr. Halilovic well and I trusted him. I was hoping that he would be able to give us a hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When you said "in terms of his command position," can you please further elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose command position do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said in your answer, Mr. Jasarevic: "In terms of his command position, he was in a position of authority." Is that what you had said earlier in your -- in response to my question to you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't understand immediately that your question was in reference to Mr. Halilovic. You see, Mr. Halilovic represented an authority that went unquestioned by any member of the army at the moment or any of the brigade members. I expected that he would be the only person with sufficient authority to -- to bear on the commander of the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what exactly is it that you asked him to do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably can't remember the details, but the crux of the matter was that I had been told that Mr. Deljkic was being kept at the command of the 10th Brigade, that he was being physically abused, humiliated, and so on. If possible, I said, "Please try to get involved to -- to help this person."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason that Mr. Deljkic himself had been chosen to be physically abused by this particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I object there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The witness said that he was abused by certain members of it, and I object to the comment that he was chosen to be abused by this brigade. The witness has been quite clear in saying that most of the brigade was fine and that there were some difficult individuals, so that question needs to be more specific, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But I believe that when the Prosecution said "the brigade," it means some members of the brigade, not the whole brigade. And by the way, Ms. Chana, maybe I missed it from yesterday's proceedings. Could you tell us about the time frame of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I will ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was when this took place? This Deljkic incident, as I call it.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. It certainly occurred before I was appointed chief of administration, so it was while I was still chief of a department within the security administration. It may have been June 1993, but I'm afraid I can't remember the specific date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'll go back to my -- my question: Why was it that certain members of this brigade had chosen Mr. Deljkic to abuse? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly don't, but I have my assumptions. Mr. Amir Deljkic, in terms of where he lived, where he resided, was quite near the command of the 10th Brigade. That might be one aspect, to my mind. Secondly, they knew that Mr. Deljkic was with the security service of the 1st Corps, and they must have assumed that anything that the security service knows about certain devious forms of behaviour by members of the 10th Brigade -- as I say, their conclusion was probably that this information was being forwarded to Mr. Deljkic and that Mr. Deljkic was in possession of this information. In my opinion, this was some sort of revenge against Mr. Deljkic for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now I would like to show you a document. Its 65 ter number is 162, it's 01474764, and that would be MFI209.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I please give the witness the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, would you please look at this document and tell us, is that your signature at the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what is this document about generally? And then we'll go into the substance of it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document that I spoke about some minutes ago. I was wrong about the date. This is early July, so that's before I was appointed the administration chief, and this is the document that I had in mind when I said the things I said a while ago. This is an official note that I produced myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this is on the 3rd of July, 1993; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It documents the conversation you had with Chief of Staff, Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was probably not able to quote the entire conversation, but it corresponds with the general meaning of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise to the witness for interrupting. He doesn't know what the problem is. But Mr. Halilovic can't see this on the screen. The Defence now can, but the accused was unable to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll ask Ms. Usher to check.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. We had a technical hitch there. As I was saying, that this is -- it's a document of the conversation you had with Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And if you look at the document in which you said -- you requested Sefer -- "I asked Sefer to intercede with Musan Topalovic, aka Caco, and Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, that Amir Deljkic, member of the military security service of the 1st Corps be freed. In fact, I was informed that Mr. Amir Deljkic had been unlawfully arrested by Musan Topalovic, aka Caco's men, and that he had been savagely maltreated physically and practically beaten up." Then you go on to say: "I knew that Mr. Sefer Halilovic would sway Caco through Celo. So I rang up and asked him to intercede to set Deljkic free. On 3rd July 1993, Sefer promised to do something. He said he would try. However, the next day, when I rang Sefer up again and asked him to save Deljkic because his life is in danger, Sefer replied to me in a fairly rough manner, saying that he didn't want to intercede for anyone individually. Even on the previous day, Mr. Sefer was more anxious to know who had informed me about what was being done to Deljkic than concerned by what was being done to him or thinking that he should be helped. On that -- on the basis of all of this, I concluded that what Caco and his villains were doing to officers from the 1st Corps command suited him perfectly, especially when the person in question was a member of the military security service, Amir Deljkic." Do you confirm the information which I've just read out, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that I produced the document. I have to say, however, that this obviously contains my own comments. This is an official note. It's a very important kind of document for the military security, especially given my position at the time, chief of counterintelligence. In my desire to help Mr. Deljkic, I have taken a slightly emotional approach to the problem. I'm not sure that you could state that Mr. Halilovic was unwilling to help. I quoted these two things. The first time round when we talked, he told me he would try. This is probably true. I don't think I just made this up. And in the second conversation, he probably replied that he did not wish to intercede on -- on the behalf of any one individual. This is probably also true. The last passage is probably a conclusion, Your Honours, and I believe it contains some emotional elements, all with the objective of providing assistance for Mr. Deljkic. I can't challenge the entire document, but certain emotional aspects of the document may be a trifle over-emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But nevertheless, these were your conclusions at the time, and you documented them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I object to leading. Your Honour, the witness has given his answers. They're out there now. They can't be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I believe the witness has answered your question before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, when you state - and that's at the -- the last couple of lines in this particular document - I would like you to assist Their Honours as to what you meant when you said, "On the basis of all this, I concluded that what Caco and his villains were doing to officers of the 1st Corps command suited him perfectly." What -- can you please assist us in telling us how is it that you came to this particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can tell, if you look at the date, this occurred immediately after what happened between the 2nd and 3rd of July, the incident caused by members of the 9th Brigade, their attack against the operations centre of the General Staff. This conversation ensued on the following day, as you can tell. There were different bits of information floating about around me. Unofficially, I mean. Hearsay, not what I heard in the office. People generally tended to express their opinions in ways that were not entirely sober and sometimes without valid arguments. My impression was, as I said earlier, that the only real authority with power to do anything in relation to those brigades was Mr. Sefer Halilovic, bearing in mind first and foremost his reputation as the army's leading person. It was only natural that I should expect such a person of authority to be able to do something. If it turns out that he was unable to do anything, I couldn't think of anyone else who might. Since I failed in resolving that issue, I provided this comment at the end of this document. It is an emotional conclusion that I drew; namely, that Mr. Sefer was simply unwilling because it was probably convenient for him, also in view of the incident the previous day, the attack against the operations centre. So this is a product of my own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And Mr. Rasim Delic, was he not the -- the head of the army at that time? Why didn't you approach him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the head of the army, but I'm not sure if he was in Sarajevo on that particular day. He would spend many days at the forward command post in Kakanj. You will understand, given my position at the time, I was not the administration chief but, rather, the chief of one of its departments. I did not have an open line of communication with the army commander. I felt personally closer and was inclined to trust Mr. Sefer Halilovic much more, bearing in mind also the fact that Mr. Sefer Halilovic would have been better able to achieve something with the commanders of those two brigades, given the authority that he had. That's one aspect of the entire matter. Secondly, I'm not sure if that tallies with the date on the document, but I did have some information, again based on information that was coming in from the security service of the 1st Corps, and some information from the Ministry of the Interior indicating that Mr. Delic was not sufficiently respected by the brigades to have any influence over them at all. So that would constitute some sort of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, was Mr. Sefer Halilovic respected by these brigades?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic was respected by all the brigades and all the commanders, as I've said already. He was the army's first man. He enjoyed an enormous amount of authority. He certainly was respected across the board. Now, what happened here, were there perhaps some reservations with regard to the breaches of discipline by these brigades, and perhaps this was expressed in an unfavourable way, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: You said you had information about these two -- two particular brigades I'm talking about, the 9th and the 10th. What were the sources of that information?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that the source of the information, the most important information, were the military security service of the 1st Corps and institutions of the Ministry for Internal Affairs, primarily the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how would this information be relayed to you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attached importance to written information. First of all, probably there were oral -- there was also oral information from meetings and so on, but I based my position on information which was contained in documents which came from the 1st Corps Security Service and the State Security Service. I cannot recall specifically this information, but I know that such information existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the general nature of this information? What kind of information was filtering through to you about these two particular brigades?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information mostly pertained to violations of military discipline by individuals or certain parts of these brigades and sometimes their commanders. This was qualified in that period as being a deviation from the system of command and control, which is characteristic for a military organisation. I'm talking about control and command, in which the principle is of the singleness of command, military obedience, and the execution of orders from superiors. These are the main principles, main -- the mainstay of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than this military indiscipline and what you allege about not following orders, was there any other information which was coming through to you about these two brigades which was obviously of some concern?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Information came which provided different indications of deviant conduct by individuals from those brigades. Individuals from those brigades and their commanders demonstrated reactions towards individuals which were not quite proper, not in the trenches -- that was inappropriate for behaviour in trenches during defence of the town. A second characteristic of their dissatisfaction, based on the information that I received, was very often demonstrated in relation to members of MUP. They thought that members of the MUP were privileged in relation to them, that they were better equipped, and that they were not actually participating in the fighting. That's how they put it. And perhaps a third point, if it's not contained in the first point that I mentioned, is that they had their own convictions, and this was something that bothered all the brigades, all the army members on the lines, that individuals through certain connections were able to secure their removal or being taken away. So they described that occurrence with a certain term, "podrumasi," people who were in the cellars. This is something which disturbed individuals in these brigades. So this would be the gist of their feelings or their sense of injustice. I'm speaking conditionally. This is how they felt at that time possibly. Of course, they did not think out properly the way to resolve this issue which they believed was unjustly dealt with, and that is why they resorted several times on -- to collecting or assembling all these individuals from the street or from cafes, wherever they found them. And it could be said that they took them to the front lines through the application of force. However, in the 10th Brigade, this was more drastic. We had information that in the 10th Brigade people were being physically abused.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What else would -- any other specific instances of this deviant behaviour that you can give us before I show you a document?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one case, for example, and I recall that very well, that members of the 9th Brigade either stole or seized - I can't really remember the particulars - a vehicle from a unit of the French UNPROFOR. After these gentlemen reacted to this from this UNPROFOR unit, after they complained to President Izetbegovic, he requested that Commander Delic resolve this question and that the vehicle be returned to the French because it was creating a negative image about our army. Delic later asked me to do this. He asked if I was able to do anything about this. I understood this as a task given to me. And through some steps that I and through some steps that I carried out, I managed to have the security chief of the brigade -- of the 9th Brigade, Mr. Tomo Juric -- Tomislav Juric, to come to my office, and Celo personally. Your Honours, I think that I mentioned yesterday that it was possible to have communication with Mr. Ramiz Delic [as interpreted] from time to time, and I managed to do so sporadically. I don't know what were all the skills that I used during that conversation to cajole Mr. Delic to return this vehicle, and I managed to do this. I don't believe that any other approach would have been successful except for this approach that I adopted, a conversation between two professionals, two soldiers, and so on. And perhaps an hour later they drove this vehicle in front of my administration building. The vehicle was still -- the paint on the vehicle was still wet. It was white and it had been painted some drab military colour. The paint was still wet when they returned it. So we have an incident here as well as the way this incident was resolved. I remember very well that I was -- I encountered him on the street. He was on his way to the administration building. It was a younger man. He's the son of a well-known Sarajevo musician, Avdo Smajlovic, so his last name is Smajlovic. I don't know his first name. And he told me that he wanted to come, that he had heard about me, that he had been taken to dig trenches by the 10th Brigade. And he was very downhearted about this, exhausted, and of course I accepted that because it was very difficult to receive any kind of information, especially from or about the 10th Brigade. This gentleman told me - this was on the street - I didn't make a record of this, but for me this was telling information because he told me some things about how the people from the 10th Brigade were gathering people and taking them to dig trenches. He said -- he told me how they were finding them on the street. Somebody would be perhaps on their way to buy bread or they would be in a cafe or a restaurant or something. It could be anywhere, and they would just pick up that person simply as if they were catching criminals. They would take them away and -- unprepared, not paying attention to the footwear the person was wearing or the clothing they were wearing, whether they were appropriately dressed for the weather conditions. They would just take them to dig trenches, regardless of whether they were healthy or -- or sick. This is mostly what they did. A person should keep this in mind. He completed his shift - that's what he said - I don't know whether this was five days or ten days. I don't know how long they would keep these people to dig trenches and then they would release them. And that is how he was released too. These are two illustrations from direct conversations, and there were many such examples, many more such examples from written documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And I will show you some of those documents in due course, but can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the court deputy could give us a number of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the meantime I think I will give you the -- the document is -- 65 ter number is 168. It's 04036176, MFI210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is the previous document. We don't have an MFI number yet. That is, the document 163. What is -- what is the MFI number for that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's 209, Your Honour, I believe. This is the next document I'm going to show the -- the witness, but not just yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, was it common knowledge, these activities of the 9th and the 10th Brigade, this -- this -- what you have now described to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's, in my submission, a meaningless question. The witness is entitled to say who he communicated with about it and who he heard it from, but to ask whether it was common knowledge, in my submission, it's just too broad and it's not a question he's in a position to answer. Unless his expertise in the knowledge of the rest of Sarajevo is established. Obviously that can't be done. He can establish -- he can give evidence about where he heard it and who he told, and that's relevant material, but that's all, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness already testified about how he gathered this information, and then this is a question for the next layer, that is, whether it's common knowledge for the people to know about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, well, your, I think you have characterised the question accurately. But that's what the difficulty is. It's not a question that this witness can answer from his own knowledge. It's difficult to see how he, as a responsible official, acting in an official capacity, is able to comment on what was common knowledge and what wasn't. If he was asked what -- whether it was circulated within his circles, in the military security, of course he could answer that. In other words, if that material was classified in some way or not classified, that's clearly relevant. What my friend means by "common knowledge" is not clear, but one can see what use might be attempted to be made of it later. So I just want to be clear what the -- the question has to be confined so that it's meaningful in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that's the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness was present during that time, during that period. He testified his way of knowing this knowledge. Then the Prosecutor asked a follow-up question, that -- whether everybody knows about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But that's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is it's -- you -- Your Honour might as well ask me that question. I'd have an opinion and Mr. Jasarevic would have an opinion about it. But that's all it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's just an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We believe that we'll allow the witness to express his opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Most obliged, Your Honour. The witness was the chief of military security at the time, so I think his -- his answer would have a little bit more value than my learned Defence counsel's opinion on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, was it common knowledge, these activities of the 9th and 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, once again, I object, and I do -- I object to the merging of common knowledge of the 9th and the 10th together. My learned friend has persisted in -- well, I won't say "deliberately," but not in distinguishing one from another. The witness distinguished and made it quite clear that there are allegations of beatings and so on by the 10th, whereas with the 9th he's referred to the theft of the UNPROFOR vehicle. Now, this question run it is two things together in an impermissible way. The 10th may have one reputation; the 9th may have a different reputation. And so my friend needs to distinguish -- as Your Honours have allowed the question to be asked, I won't argue that. But it needs to be distinguished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard evidence about the 10th Brigade, but I'm afraid that we did not hear any evidence about 9th Brigade at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two things. One is I think yesterday I did point out to Your Honours that some of these objections and the lengthy explanations that the objections are made are inappropriate before a witness while he's in court. Learned counsel can allude to some certain matters. And certainly, Your Honours, the witness had talked about the brigades, but I take your point and will ask him about one brigade at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's go over both the brigades, but I take your point and I will ask him at one brigade at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go brigade by brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I want to distinguish between the two brigades, the 9th and the 10th. Can you now, before I ask you whether the -- this information was common knowledge, can you tell us, what had you heard about the activities or the negative conduct of the 9th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, already in the description of the round-up of citizens from the street and from cafes and other places for digging of trenches, I spoke about that already, and it was characteristic for the 9th and 10th Brigades. But the members of the 9th Brigade were a little bit more lenient in this matter than the members of the 10th Brigade, which I described in examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Jasarevic, was this conduct of the 9th Brigade first common knowledge in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from the 1st Corps. There were also some things coming in from the General Staff counter-intelligence unit, from the counter-intelligence unit of the administration, and their information was based on operative work. And as an official responsible, in view of the position I had, I took such information into account and attached importance to this information. I did not organise for this information to be treated in bulletins and to be put into reports and included into reports which were forwarded to the superior command. I didn't want to include things that came through unofficial channels or based on things that were being talked about on the street. I can't even remember all of the things that were being said at the time, and it's not something that I would stand by 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What things were being said on the streets?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't sit on the street --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I withdraw the objection in light of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, carry on, Mr. Jasarevic. What were you saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- perhaps, Your Honour, I do object. I think at a certain point, Your Honour, remoteness sets in. When the witness, who's the head of military security, is called about killings that take place in September in Herzegovina, to ask him what he heard on the street in July or June is really just getting so speculative and vague, especially given the answers that he has given so far, to be just too remote from the question that we have to consider here. And in my submission, this line of questioning now is just -- it's really just fishing. And -- well, look, I object to it on the grounds of remoteness, as, frankly, the witness himself seems to be commenting. So I just raise the objection now that we -- we're really getting into an area where we're -- there's nothing concrete about what's being asked, and the answers themselves are quite appropriate. The witness is answering as he's asked and he's entitled to answer as he's asked. What I'm submitting is that he shouldn't be asked these questions. Let him be asked about incidents or concrete things, if there are such things, and things that are relevant to the case. But as to what was being said on the street, Your Honour, it's just too vague to be meaningful, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I believe that it's not proper for you to interrupt in the middle of the witness's answer. Secondly, I think that -- I believe that the incidents that happened before the specific case we are hearing has some relevance to what happened later on, because I believe that it's part of the Prosecution's case. Thirdly, I believe that the Prosecution has already asked some specific questions concerning a particular incident already. Then he will ask some general reflections, maybe on the streets, maybe in some other areas, on this issue. And the witness is going to answer that question, which may be not unfavourable to your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm bound by Your Honour's ruling on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, witness, you may continue to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot remember or talk about what was assumed to have been talked about on the street, in view of the duties I performed. My positions and my views were based on official information, written information of the 1st Corps primarily, and there was enough of such information, also written information from the security service, and possibly there were probably such indications as well or such information from the sector -- from the General Staff counter-intelligence sector, which turned its information into official notes which would then reach me in that form. From this distance, it's very hard for me to remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, did you ever have occasion to speak to Mr. Halilovic about these matters?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, except for this conversation regarding the Deljkic problem and how to resolve that. Otherwise, I really don't recall whether I did or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, sometime ago in your testimony you -- you said before this Court that Halilovic was the main man - I think that was the word that you used - that he was the number one in the army. Do you know what the relationship was between Mr. Delic and Mr. Halilovic? Did you have any knowledge of this, the relationship between the two men?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Delic, after that, were my superior officers. I am a soldier, and I accepted them as authorities superior to me. I didn't want to and I didn't have any option of dealing or thinking about the relationship between the two of them. There were information -- there was information in written material from which you could decide that there was a certain animosity there. Of course, at working meetings in the operations centre or at some other working meetings, at the staff, you could tell that a certain number of people were more inclined towards Mr. Halilovic because he had been there longer and they knew him better, and I felt that this was quite natural in a way, that they were closer to him. There was also a number of people who knew Delic from before, and they were in favour of him coming. So in that sense, they might have been more inclined towards Mr. Delic, because as an officer, he was more qualified. Conditionally speaking, there was also a third group which was mindful of the institution of person number one, of the post. First of all, we had the Chief of the General Staff or the Main Staff, and then in the second period we had the title Commander of the General Staff or the Main Staff. So in that sense, I'm using the term "number-one man." Throughout that period, what was important, from the aspect of my position, was that their relationship did not result in any negative aspects in the managing of the staff or in combat activities. It was just something that could -- it was not something that was obvious. I didn't acknowledge that there was any such animosity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But the ones who -- would they show their loyalty to Halilovic in any -- any way, the ones who still liked Halilovic over Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't that pronounced. It was a more flexible situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like now to take you to this document that I've already --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is MFI210, Your Honour. Can I give the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell me about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you seen this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. My learned friend is now about, I think, to ask the question I want to ask, so ... Sorry, I thought she was but she's not. Your Honours, I'm sorry, it's just that, given the proofing notes here, Your Honour will notice what the -- what appears to be the status of this document. So the witness ought to be given the chance to indicate whether he knows the document, first of all, and then move from that position onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know this document, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document was produced at a time when I was not chief of administration. I can tell by the handwriting that this is my predecessor's, Mr. Muslimovic's signature. He is here, assigning this task to the analysis sector to process this and include it in the bulletin to be sent to the group of superiors that I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But at proofing, you had mentioned that you know the information within this document. And I'd like to take you to a certain section of this document, and that if you -- first of all, this is about the 9th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- I object to this. Why doesn't -- well, my submission is that, if there's an incident to be asked about and the witness knows about it, then of course it's relevant and just ask him about the incident. To direct him to a document that is not his, in my submission, has the evils that I raised yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We had a ruling yesterday that, if the witness does not know about this document, you could just ask a question directly to that incident which he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to use this document to remind -- to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- to see whether he can recall, because I've already asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if he knows that incident, I believe that he does not need anything to remind. If you give this document, the document -- the witness has never seen this document, that will be misleading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will put the question to him first and then I will request Your Honours whether I may show him, to remind him of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, if you don't look at the document for the time being and answer this question: Do you know whether any of Celo's men were wearing Sefer Halilovic badges?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people from our administration told me that they had heard something along these lines. There was something about this in the written reports of the 1st Corps. I personally never saw a person with a Halilovic badge on their chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But you heard they existed?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I will now take you to another document, which is MFI211. The 65 ter is 160, 04035899.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is of the same genre, and I think the witness has already discussed and talked about trench-digging.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jasarevic, who was primarily taken to dig trenches on the front line in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just not sure at the moment, is my friend showing the witness the document? Because if she is, she has to ask the question, has he seen it before. If she's not showing it to him, that's okay. I have no objection to the question that's now being asked, because there had been other questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's make that clear first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking the -- the question again. He has talked about this particular topic of trench-digging, and I wanted to show him this particular document. And before I did, I asked the question. So at this moment, he's not being shown the document, he's being asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was taken to dig trenches in the front lines in Sarajevo, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've spoken about this before, Your Honours. Persons rounded up in the streets, young people mostly, in cafes. The brigade members were riled by this, particularly so the members of these two brigades. Also, these two brigades were near the town centre, which means that they were in contact with these people who weren't directly involved in combat, so they decided to use these people at least to do some trench-digging for them, and they would later use these trenches in combat. And also, the people they referred to as cellar-dwellers, people hiding somewhere in order to avoid being sent to the front line. So these were the basic groups of people who were usually rounded up by the members of these brigades. It was typical of both groups, but I must say that the 10th Brigade was much more severe in how they went about this job than the 9th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, just to confirm, were they civilians or military? A short answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not use this document any more, but I will show the witness another document, which is MFI212, 65 ter 151, 01474907.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, before you look at this document, Mr. Jasarevic, can you tell us: Did you get any information on Sefer Halilovic, his activities?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What exactly do you have in mind? What sort of activity?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Negative activities.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got some information from the State Security Service. For the most part, this information had to do with how he treated those two brigades. I am only speaking about what I received in writing. Sometimes in these written reports one would find something being said about how he treated Commander Delic. I'm not sure, but also the state president was mentioned. I'm afraid I might go wrong, because what I'm saying is based on my memory, but these written documents exist. They were processed by the administration, included in bulletins, and sent on to superior officers. When I spoke about our operative work yesterday, the sort of work usually performed by the security service, I said, Your Honours, that we were not entitled to keep information back. If this information appeared at all relevant, we were supposed to process this information immediately. In wartime it was difficult to verify all the information received, needless to say, so whatever knowledge or information we had would invariably be forwarded higher up; otherwise, we would have been responsible for the potential consequences, if, for example, we received a bit of information and kept silent about it. So this was a regular procedure

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's look at this document. You've seen this document before. If you look at the front page, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got an objection to this document, and the objection is one of relevance. Now, this witness did, it may be, see this document, it might have passed through his hands, so he would be allowed to comment on it. And if he's permitted to go ahead, I won't object to him commenting on it, as he's entitled to do. But this appears to be different to the reputation of the 9th Brigade, the 10th Brigade, or anything like that. This just appears to be being led to the reputation of Sefer Halilovic, and he's not charged with having notice of his own bad behaviour. This seems to be an attack on the character of Halilovic. Now, I call on the Prosecutor to indicate that it's not an attack on his character and that it's got some relevance to the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document very much talks about the two brigades. It talks about many other aspects of the accused's relationships with various other people. It is extremely relevant to the Prosecution case. Your Honour, this is my examination-in-chief. The witness has seen this document. My learned friend has objected throughout, and this one, if I may be permitted to continue with it, it will become obvious because the witness had said in proofing, and it's part of the proofing notes, that he had actually prepared a draft based on this information and sent the information forward, which is what the witness just said; that he would get this information and disseminate it forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's come to the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can we look at the front page of this document. You have seen this document before. Did you do anything with the document yourself, the -- the contents of it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be allowed to say that this is not a document I produced. Secondly, I never said that I saw this document before. I am familiar with its substance, however. Also, because at the time it was produced, it was produced by the State Security Service, and the memo also includes the Supreme Command Staff and the security service. This is going on at the same time as the Trebevic I and Trebevic II operations. In my opinion, in a purely formal sense, there is a signature missing. Whoever produced this document forgot to sign it. I did tell the OTP, however - and I shall repeat it before the Trial Chamber - that the information contained in this document are a result of information provided by the military security service of the 4th Corps. And what I spoke about a while ago, the State Security Service and the corps security services, whenever they submitted a report to us at the security service administration, any reports indicating forms of behaviour that might escalate and cause serious consequences or perhaps adversely affect any decisions on how the army should be used, we would, of course, process these and produce special reports of the security administration. These were numbered, signed by the chief of administration, stamped, assigned a number, and these reports were sent higher up as official documents. But again, I must refer you back to the concept of operative information, which I believe I have already sufficiently explained in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jasarevic. Can we now, please -- is the document headed "On the Negative Conduct and Activities of Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the BH Armed Forces"? Would you confirm that's the heading of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has given a clear answer here. He said -- he never said that he'd seen the document before, so perhaps there's a misunderstanding that's happened in proofing here. I don't know. But I don't want to go and look into that issue at all. All I'd say is the witness has said that he hasn't seen -- or he says, "I never said that I saw this document before." He is familiar with its substance. If it's relevant to the Prosecution case - and my friend has given an undertaking that it is - then he can be asked about that substance, so long as it's relevant to the case. So long as it's not a mere smear, I won't object. But this document now falls into the same category as all the other ones, in which -- where the witness says he either hasn't seen it or doesn't know about it, so that the witness can be asked what he knows. Frankly, I think he's already said -- given the answer to that. But my friend now wanting to proceed with the document as she is, shouldn't be permitted to. It falls into the same category as the other ones, based on the answer which you'll see there at the -- at the top of the paragraph that's now vanished on my screen, unfortunately, because I talked so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness said that, "I never said I saw this document before. I'm familiar with its substance."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I -- may I ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may ask a question to this witness when --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- did he see this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you remember I showed you this document in proofing?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you -- what did you say at the time I showed you this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour gave a clear direction as to what could be asked. My friend can ask that, not this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Just ask the question in the way I asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document as I was being proofed here. It was shown to me by a member of the OTP. But I can't remember that I had ever seen this document prior to that. It was my established practice; you're likely to see that if you look at any of the documents that I produced. In the upper right-hand corner, wherever there was a bit of room, I would provide suggestions and hand out tasks to my subordinates. Again, I stated quite unambiguously that the substance of this document is something that I was familiar with based on my conversations with the State Security Service, with the security service of the 4th Corps, and, in part, also the 5th and 6th. This was transformed and included in a special report that I signed. The fact that the report was signed by the security administration means that I hereby accept something that the analysis sector wrote based on the primary documents that they used and sent on to the security administration, but also as a result of operative information and knowledge, which is something that we were in no position to verify at the time, and by the same token, we were in no position to be 100 per cent certain about the veracity of the information contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to the information contained in this, and I want to ask you whether this is something that was to your knowledge, because you said that your analytical department used this as a basis. I'll start at the beginning of the document by saying: "By using measures designed to protect BH Armed Forces units and commands, under the jurisdiction of the State Security Service and the Supreme Command Staff, documented factual evidence has been obtained which clearly demonstrates that Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the BH Armed Forces, Supreme Command, operated deliberately and methodically with the goal of provoking a crisis situation in BH, especially in the Sarajevo area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd seek to interrupt here. My friend is reading this into the record now. Now, Your Honours, this has gone on long enough. My friend started that question there by saying, "I'd like to take you to the information contained within this," and that was ambiguous, so I didn't object to it at the time. But then ultimately the question became simply one of reading out this document, which the witness has made quite clear when he saw it. Now, there's a legitimate line for my friend to explore in this. It's not for me to wonder about these things. But the answer having been given that he hadn't seen this document until proofing, it's just not proper to read it into the transcript and to attempt to put it to the witness in the form that's happening. So I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in the testimony, this witness said that he was familiar with the contents of this document and his report was based on the contents of this document. That is very clear. So the Prosecution could ask some questions concerning of this document or ask this witness to verify some points in this document. However, the Prosecution cannot read the whole document to this witness. Let's come to the specific incidents or contents in this document and ask this witness to verify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. The most -- one of the more important aspects of this document is -- I'll put it to Mr. Jasarevic in this way:

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you turn to page 2 of this document - this is the second paragraph on that document - it says there that, "In order to achieve this objective, Halilovic found support in the commands of units which included a large number of criminals. Their criminal actions were organised by the closest associates" --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's page 2, Your Honour. No, it's page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you with me, Mr. Jasarevic? Can you -- have you identified the chapter that I'm reading from, the paragraph? Page 1, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: "Their criminal actions were organised by closest associates who held posts in the command and control system. Every day Sefer encouraged such people to direct contacts by phone or wire radio, especially after the office of commander of the staff of the supreme command was created to obstruct their official corps commands, the 1st or the 4th Corps, and to grow independent distance themselves from and dodge any form of control by their commanders." Now, Mr. Jasarevic, in respect of that particular paragraph, was this information available to you, that this was the activities of Sefer Halilovic in respect of these criminal units?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was available to me through the document that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then I'll go on. And I'm now looking at the third paragraph, where it starts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Ms. Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have you -- are you with me on that third paragraph, that "He especially imbued" --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I didn't get your answer. Have you found that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. "He especially imbued the individuals listed hereafter with a high degree of personal animosity towards the figures mentioned above: Ramiz Delalic, aka Celo, commander of the 9th Motorised Brigade; Musan Topalovic, aka Caco, commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade; Zulfikar Alispago, commander of the so-called special detachment of the Supreme Command Staff, and individual unit commanders in the Konjic, Jablanica, and Visoko area. In doing so, he presented himself as the sole, rightful military leader who had the right concept of how to defend the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas, according to him, the figures mentioned above lacked a clear-cut defence concept and consequently conducted a policy of betrayal." Now, in respect of what I have just read out to you, were you familiar, Mr. Jasarevic, with this information?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to a certain extent, I've answered this already. Any information I received in this way, or rather, any information received by the administration which I headed, would be state security information. Statements like these and conclusions like these were binding for my department, for my administration, and me personally. We would receive this information and forward it to our superiors. That is why I am inclined to conclude that, as information goes, yes, I was familiar with this bit of information. My apologies. However, there was no way I could back this sort information as authentic, not then, not now. As the administration chief, for me, this was operative information which needed verifying. I remember, Your Honours, that this information by the State Security Service was based on their own transcripts. I didn't use their equipment; I didn't see their documents; I never listened to their tapes or indeed transcribed the conversations from those tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this information, you said, is based on transcripts and their own documents and tapes. Which transcripts, documents, and tapes would this be, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also said that I never actually saw the transcripts or the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- sorry to interrupt you. If you can please answer which -- I know you did not see them; you've already said that. But could you please tell the Court what -- upon what it was based. And you've mentioned three pieces there - documents, transcripts, and tapes. To your knowledge, what were these? That's the question, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are a result of the application of a measure known to the security services as "the secret method." This means putting taps on the phone belonging to a person under surveillance, a person whose behaviour and acts need to be investigated to attain the truth about that person. The military security service had no power to use that method. The possibility to use this method is enshrined in some of the rules governing the work of the service, and this was under the jurisdiction of the state security. I didn't see the tapes, I didn't see the equipment used, and I didn't see what certain people were listening to and transcribing. It is base on one of these documents that this report was drafted and forwarded to its end-users.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Jasarevic, we do understand that. So are you then saying this was on intercepted telephone conversations? That's what you -- before Mr. Morrissey gets up, I hear him reaching for his gun. You -- it's on intercepted telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said here that this is based on tapes and conversations which were intercepted. These would be telephone conversations which were -- I'm just confirming that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I now understand what you mean by "intercepts," or "listening in." Listening in is something that the secret services do. That means tapping people's phones. And this is a result of that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So this report is a result of that kind of work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The witness is not -- the witness is saying what he understood the source of the information given to him to be. He's not saying that these transcripts are genuine or that -- that there's any truth in it whatsoever. He's just saying what the source of his material is. And my friend shouldn't -- shouldn't lead on that topic but should just allow the witness to answer in his own way about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the witness has already answered that question. And -- Did you finish this document, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not, Your Honour. I want to put another -- another couple of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But it's high time for us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- for the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. We can continue after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I want to take you to another paragraph in this document, please, where it says: "In expressing these political ambitions..." I don't know what page yours will be. It starts with "In expressing these political ambitions..." Middle of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. "In expressing these political ambitions, with the wish of provoking a crisis which should be conducive to a conflict within the BH army and between army and MUP units, Sefer often incited the commanders of receptive units loyal to him against other commanders and their units, MUP units, and the MUP leadership. He did this by sending them a series of conspiratorial messages in succession to the effect that the MUP was about to attack their units which the commanders of the 9th Motorised Brigade, the 10th Mountain Brigade, the Deltas, and the Zulfikar detachment, accepted with complete seriousness so that they continually prepared the units for the eventuality of such clashes. He deduced hatred and discord within the most sensitive segments of the defence system, and prepared extremists under the influence of commanders devoted to him to carry out the most serious form of terror and crime in the event a clash should arise, which was demonstrated in the brutal murders of nine members of the military police and MUP 3 and in countless other cases of terror perpetrated against the residents of Sarajevo, all of which lasted over a number of months." Now, Mr. Jasarevic, may I ask first you to confirm that this was information that you had. Now, I know you've already said that -- that you cannot confirm the veracity of it, but is this information which was put forward to you and upon which you yourself made a report and sent further?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially this last part, dealing with the killing of nine members of the military police; six from the military police and three from the MUP, a total of nine. These are police officers who were killed at the end of -- with the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade. The action to deal with these people, this is part of the action Trebevic I and Trebevic II, and this is the part that I had indicated. And this is a summary or an overview of the information in its final, most intensive phase of the operations Trebevic I and Trebevic II, when the negative occurrences in the 9th and 10th Brigade were being dealt with. As I said before, this is an information and there was no possibility to check on what is there. Except for the killing of these nine police officers, this is something that is already known to myself and to others, so there can be no doubt about that. As for the other things, the same things applied to this particular thing as to all the other information that I spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Jasarevic, when it says, "did this by sending them a series of conspiratorial messages," there a star and there's a footnote. Can you see that footnote, please? Are you -- are you --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this footnote says: "Sefer warned Delalic about the alleged attack by MUP units on 13 October 1993. The one who told me about that illness, you know", and it quotes: "The one who told me about that illness, you know, and that" --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- "this is rather serious. In any event, appropriate medicine should be prepared and, if need be, if things get worse, it should be applied. In any event, therapy. Get the medicine ready and that's it." What does this footnote mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Excuse me, witness. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise to the witness for intervening there. Well, Your Honour, this is being read into the transcript. The witness is now being asked to comment on a footnote. It's completely against the spirit of what was -- what was ruled on earlier on. I've got some other objections I want to raise, but I'll leave them until we're finished with this document. But Your Honour will see that my friend is just reading the whole thing, or most of it, into the transcript, despite Your Honour's ruling, frankly. And as to taking the footnote, this is commentary on the document. Now, my friend knows and Your Honour has -- I took Your Honour to rule that the witness can comment on whether he received particular information or not, and Your Honours made a ruling to that effect. But to ask him to comment on what that footnote means when he said what he's already said about it, in my submission, is impermissible. It's getting him to comment on this document. There's been reference to the -- to a document that he brought into being, and frankly it would be appropriate if there -- you know, if that document is around, to refer to that rather than this. But that's the objection I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Chana, do you have anything to say on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness is familiar with documents, is familiar with the way they are framed. He's already stated to the Court, Your Honour, that this is -- based on this information, he drafts his own and sends his up the line. And this footnote has a quote in it, and I would like to ask him what does that mean in the sense of when it's quoted in that way. I could clearly ask him the question: Is it a quote from an intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that sometimes you need to ask a direct question to this witness without quoting whatever is said in this document, because later on we might have a discussion on whether to admit it, this document, into the evidence or not. Since we used this document very extensively, so there might be a chance for this document to be admitted into the evidence. If so, there's no need for you to read the whole paragraph of this document to this witness. As for the footnotes, well, frankly speaking, I'm also curious about, you know, the meaning of this footnote, but you could ask him a direct question to this point rather than quoting whatever is said in the document as well as in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be very happy to ask him a direct question, but there'll be no doubt that counsel will stand on his feet and say it's a leading question. So whichever way I go, Your Honour, counsel seems to be determined to put his cross-examination during my examination-in-chief. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the Defence counsel has full opportunity to cross-examine this witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, does this footnote mean to you that this was a quote from a telephone conversation? If you look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this has been placed in quotation marks and is a quotation of a recorded telephone conversation. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, without having to read the document, if I just -- if you just keep looking at the document, I'll ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before that happens, Your Honour, I've got another matter to raise. Your Honours, if the source of this is telephone conversations, then Your Honours' ruling at the start of the trial as to evidentiary matters concerning the best-evidence rule ought to be considered. You know, we were served with this material late. The Prosecution, because the trial was imminent, was permitted, as Your Honours have indicated, in a ruling, to use this material. They are doing so now without providing the chain of custody. They're just using it. But now it emerges that it's based on something else, or might well be based on something else, and the Prosecution ought to indicate to you whether they have any such telephone tapes, which would be the best evidence; or failing that, transcripts by people who listened to those tapes, if that's the next best evidence. The Prosecutor ought to reveal now whether they have such material, and if they do, they ought to tell why we don't have it and why it's not being put in evidence properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a legitimate question being put by the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, for this witness -- all I've asked is whether he understands this is to be a telephone intercept, and that's the only question. He's answered that question, and I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But my question is: What's the relevance, this piece of the information, to our case?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The relevance is, Your Honour, in the context of the criminality of the -- of the brigades, and Halilovic's knowledge. The relevance is extremely clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe I could sense it at a later stage, but at this moment it seems to me that I fail to understand the relevance of this footnote. So you did not answer my question -- I mean, the Defence counsel's question in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have those intercepts or some other records concerning the information of this piece of document?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, full disclosure has been made to the Defence as to the -- the exhibits and -- that we're going to be using. And as of now, I cannot confirm or deny whether we have these particular telephone conversations. This document is based on a collection of information, and for my purposes and this witness, I'm dealing only with that, that this is a report being collected through intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you neither have the report written by this witness based on this document. You don't have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I have another report which I'll be coming to. If I am allowed to finish my examination-in-chief, all will become clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm expecting that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you still don't have an answer to the question, and the question is: Has the Prosecutor got those tapes or not? Now, there's a non-responsive answer so far. It doesn't matter what my friend has in mind for this witness or not. The question is - and it's a clear one - do they have these tapes and/or such transcripts? It's no use to say that disclosure has been made to the Defence and that the Prosecution are very fair and that they have the carriage of the Prosecution. Of course, all of those things may be right. But Your Honour's question and my question are simple and easy to answer. They're easy to answer. Unlike the question the other day that we had, this one can be answered by yes or no. Do they have these telephone transcripts or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, Ms. Chana has promised us that she will check it after today's sitting, and this witness will stay here at least for another day. And before we finish this witness, I believe that I could get a definite answer to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't press the matter any further. Would it be acceptable that the Prosecutor give us a report to that effect before court starts tomorrow? And that way we don't waste time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are going to sit until 7.00, you know. I think we need some time for supper and for rest, you know. Maybe before the start of your cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, that's acceptable to me. But I need that information before I begin. But yes, I accept that, Your Honour. I'll say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So your answer was, witness, that it -- it is -- would be a telephone intercept, and it's a direct quotation, and I think you confirmed that in respect of that particular footnote. Were you aware that Sefer Halilovic was inciting commanders of units loyal to him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except for the reports which I received of such a nature, I had some doubt or concerns that the consequences could be quite substantial.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. For the time being I'll move right on. Now, can you tell me: In late July 1993, you had a meeting. Did you have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? What kind of meeting? Could you just please clarify this a little bit more. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, of the Council for Protection of the Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I confirm that there was such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And could you tell us who was present, please, at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting at the level of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, attended by the members of the Presidency. I don't know if all of them attended it. It was a meeting of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. That is the name of that body. It was headed by Mr. Mirko Pejanovic. One of the people who initiated this meeting was actually I myself, after I took on the post of chief of security. We were assessing the security situation in the town, also the extremely complex problem of the defence of the city --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- lack of discipline in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- Jasarevic, I'm sorry to interrupt.
