Before we go on to the substance of this meeting, I would like you to please inform me who was at this meeting, other than Mr. Pejanovic and yourself. Of course I mean -- I mean the more superior -- the supreme -- the higher-level commanders and political...

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiators or the participants, on the one hand, at the meeting were Mr. Rasim Delic, as the commander of the army; Mr. Bakir Alispahic, as the Minister of Internal Affairs; and I myself, as the head of the security administration of the Main Staff. In a way, we reported on the increasing problems amongst the units --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which were not within the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would still -- I haven't finished with the people who attended. Were there members of the Presidency there? Was Alija Izetbegovic there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I thought I mentioned that. Yes, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was present, also Mr. Stjepan Kljuic was present. I remember that Mr. Muhamed Filipovic was present. I think that the president of the Centar municipality, Mr. Kambur or Kamber, was present. I can't recall the rest, but that is more the composition of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I really can't remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was discussed at this meeting? And this is in relation, of course, to the situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I started to talk about that. The growing problems with respect to the conduct primarily of the 9th and 10th Brigades was discussed, as well as the absence of discipline as a problem in the town, which potentially posed a danger due to which the whole town could fall. All the information that we had had to be considered, and we could not underestimate this problem, because if we allowed these two brigades to continue to be undisciplined, we would have a massacre which, by scale, would be greater than the one in Zenica. And that is why we asked that the Presidency and the Supreme Command of the state states its position on this problem, because the risk at some other level could be quite great, the risk of making any kind of decision was quite great, because the consequences of that could be catastrophic. And that is why we wanted the Presidency or that body participates in the resolution of that problem which was affecting the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who put this information forward to the council? Who spoke about it? Who actually talked about this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - I cannot be quite certain about it - but I think Mr. Rasim Delic spoke first, followed by Mr. Alispahic, the MUP minister. I also addressed the meeting. The present members of the council and the Presidency also addressed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what kind of conduct did you place before the council in respect of these two brigades?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem boiled down to the fact that the brigades, to a certain extent, were outside of the command-and-control system of the 1st Corps. We expressed the concern that these two brigades, their command or some sections of that command, could affect the other units in the town. Also, based on reports that we mentioned so far, it was not clear to us what the role of Mr. Sefer Halilovic was, and even though we didn't have definite information that had been checked about his having a direct influence or being in direct command, we could still talk about the lack of discipline amongst those units but we could not do anything. In view of the consequences, we could not risk anything. And this is why we asked for the top leadership of the state and the military to take a position regarding this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So was there a suggestion that Sefer Halilovic might have been de facto commander of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has to endeavour not to lead. Furthermore, that's an ultimate issue question, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is a leading question. You may put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said, "It was not clear to us what the role of Mr. Sefer Halilovic was." Can you elaborate on that, please, as to -- what was it that you were not sure about? In respect -- the role in respect of what?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am talking about whether I was certain or not. This was 11 years ago, so I cannot remember all the particulars regarding the views of the others or what Mr. Alispahic or Mr. Delic said. I myself absolutely had no definite information about the direct involvement of Mr. Halilovic in all of this. But the information, the reports that we had, which we talked about today and yesterday, provided a kind of basis to take such information seriously. They were operative -- this was operative data. It was something that was not checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were these views expressed - and I'm not talking about your own personal one, but by others at this meeting - about Sefer Halilovic's role and their understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an absolutely definite answer to that question because I cannot really remember that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you yourself give any personal recommendations to this meeting as to what ought to be done?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I commented on one act to partially resolve this problem, and that was to bring in the chief of the 10th Mountain Brigade, Mr. Pecar, his last name was Pecar, where - this was earlier actually, even before I took up this duty - where this had taken on a provocative aspect for that unit. I was even of the opinion that this was something that provoked the incident between the 2nd and 3rd of July, and I even described this detail that it was my opinion that this problem cannot be resolved in that way, that this way or manner of resolving this problem could provoke far-reaching effects affecting the position of the units and the defence of the town. I discussed this at the meeting and requested that, from the aspect of security, not going into any military particulars - the tactical operative details, because the commander was present and he is more in charge of that aspect of the question - that actually we needed to approach this -- the resolution of this problem in a very responsible way. That's what I remember saying now, but this was a long time ago and there are too many things to recall about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What concerns were expressed in solving this problem? What were the other concerns that this meeting generally had in solving the problem of the 9th and the 10th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the method selected was the most reasonable method to be employed at the time simply because most of those present understood what the problem was, and for everyone the problem of actually defending the town was foremost. If an error occurred in that area, consequences would be far-reaching and disastrous. This was a predominant note with all of those who were involved in the meeting. I can't remember any further details.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what was the -- the defence of Sarajevo, can you elaborate on that, please. What was concerning the meeting about dealing with these units vis-a-vis the defence of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th and the 10th Brigades were strong units. Roughly speaking, their strengths -- their respective strengths were between 5.000 and 6.000 people altogether. The 10th Brigade held the southern and the south-eastern sector of the town defence, the slopes of the -- of Mount Trebevic, and the 10th held most of the northern sector, roughly speaking, the Centar municipality. In a liberal estimate, this was about one-fourth or even as much as one-third of the entire town's defence, of the defence line of the entire town. This was the greatest concern, the greatest problem; namely, our fear that any unwarranted mistakes might provoke the commands of these units, units that were, as they were, conditionally speaking, outside the control and command system of the 1st Corps. At least, that's how we put it at the time. Again, I'm must say "conditionally speaking," though I must say they were entirely -- I can't say they were entirely outside the system of command and control, but in part they were. This required a serious approach by the army, by the Ministry of the Interior, by the authorities and by the politicians. A decision had to be taken on what course of action to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Why couldn't Rasim Delic call them in? What did he say at the meeting in respect of that. He's the head of the army. He's the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I am speaking from memory. I can't quote a single thing, but as far as I remember, speaking of the meetings which I then began to attend, meetings of the Main Staff, in my capacity as administration chief, Commander Delic spoke about the problem of poor discipline of some of the units. When he spoke about these matters, he said that he had tried to get in touch with those units through the corps commander. He said something along the same lines at the meeting, and he said it didn't work. I'm not sure if the time frame is the same, but it was at about the same time that members of the 10th Mountain Brigade rounded up his son, a young man of about 20 years of age who was a member of the army. They took him back to their base and beat him up properly. He somehow managed to escape and he was assisted in this by UNPROFOR. During that time, Delic tried to get through to the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade, but as far as I'm aware, to no avail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, you testified that the method selected was the most reasonable one and you also said that a decision has to be taken on what course of action to take. What is the method selected at this meeting and what is the decision made at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the method, or part of the method, should I say, was the request itself and the meeting to have a discussion at that level and for a decision to be taken at that level. That's what I have in mind. So that the problem would not be dealt with exclusively at Main Staff level or at MUP level or at 1st Corps level, which would have been a perfectly natural situation under a different set of circumstances, where discipline was good, where there was subordination. Now, in a hypothetical situation of that nature, it would have been dealt with by the 1st Corps only.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were any minutes taken at this meeting? Was there any written memoranda produced?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So as the meeting ended, what was the final conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the three of us were assigned -- were given instructions, actually, to review the plan to be proposed to the president on how to deal with this problem, to advise the corps commander, and to look at the various possibilities to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you please define "the three of us." Who are the three of you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three of us who attended the meeting. In terms of their respective positions, first and foremost, the reference was to Commander Delic and Minister Alispahic, but I was there too. And part of this assignment certainly applied to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And when you said "deal with the problem," what were the parameters of the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic parameter was that there had been deviation from the standard system of command and control. This was likely to pose a danger leading to the fall of the town, and this would have resulted in disaster, in a massacre of probably dozens of thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: To put it another way: Who were the people who you were supposed to devise a plan about? Who was included amongst the tasking that you were to make the plan about?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, at the implementation stage, things were taken one step at a time, bearing in mind all along the sensitive nature of the issue, bearing in mind the need to make no mistakes and not to disclose the nature of our objective. Three groups were set up to deal with the problem. The first group in charge of the control -- command and control of the entire operation --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before I get into the detail of the operation itself, I just want to know what was your parameters of your tasking. Who was it? Was it the 9th Brigade? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, no, no, no. My friend -- well, I object to it as leading. I have won't make a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, can we -- you said -- and I -- before we continue with other matters, you said "to look into the problem." Now, I want to know, who was the problem? Who were you looking into? We'll go into the details of the various units later, but who was it that you were looking into as you were given your taskings?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were looking into was acts of indiscipline predominantly by the 9th and the 10th Brigades. However, also other information was reviewed --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this information was in reference to some other units. Just what I was about to say. Reference was made to some other units, such as the Delta unit, the Zulfikar unit. I'm not sure of any other units or not. In actual fact, there was concerns about evaluating the sum total of these difficulties. We had no reliable parameters on what influence exactly they exercised over the other units that were part of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than these units, was there anybody else you were looking into?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these reports, a plan was drawn up to deal with this issue, and Mr. Sefer Halilovic was certainly involved in his official capacity as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So now, you were saying -- before we get on to exactly the detail of this, I want to remain in chronological order and I want to take you on to another subject matter. I'm now into late August 1993. Do you know any military operation which was planned during that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you aware there was a meeting in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know of an operation called Operation Neretva 93?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the operation and its scope became clear to me gradually, at a later stage. As for how the operation was planned and conducted, I knew practically nothing and I also knew nothing about its results.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you required to put a -- make a security assessment for this forthcoming operation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. I wish I had taken part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would it have been normal for you to make a security assessment for military operations?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you allocate a military security operative -- a security officer, I'm sorry, for the operation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for the operation. I was not even aware of the operation to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Namik Dzankovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an officer in the administration of which I was head.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did he have anything to do with this operation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I want to show you a document. It's 163, 65 -- it's 213, MFI213, 04035783. Do you see this document, Mr. Jasarevic? Is it signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't sign this document. My signature is not here. I was probably away at the time. But I am familiar with the substance of this document, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what does this document in fact do or say?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was requested, as the chief of the administration, to assign one of my men to a team that was to be led by Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, Sefer Halilovic, and this team would be on its way to the Neretva Valley. This team was named, as I was to remember later, inspection team. One of the senior officers - I can't remember who specifically, whether General Rasuljevic or General Rifat Bilajac - okay, they were not generals at the time, but they were later promoted - there was an oral communication or something else perhaps. I think there was a even a conclusion from an operations centre meeting at the General Staff that a team like this should be set up and that I should assign one of my officers to the team. I would like to point out what was particularly important for me in the whole thing: No conditions were imposed, no criteria as to who this officer should be or what his tasks would be. Coincidentally, Mr. Dzankovic requested several days prior to go to the Neretva Valley to look for his mother who was there among the refugees, among the countless refugees fleeing Mostar after an HVO onslaught. They were fleeing down the river, and he had received word that his mother was ill, that there was something wrong with her legs. Obviously I allowed him to leave. Then I was requested to assign one of my own officers to the team. As no conditions were specified, no requirements, and I didn't know what the requests -- what the tasks would be, I made a rational decision to appoint Dzankovic, since he was already out in the field. I was not aware of his specific whereabouts, so this document was sent to the commands of the 4th and 6th Corps, who then located him on the ground through their own teams. I got in touch with them, told them to find the man and tell him that he should join an inspection team led by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was he a professional security officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, before that question is persisted with, I'm sorry, we have a technical problem. I don't believe Mr. Halilovic had in front of him the relevant order on that occasion, and unfortunately we didn't either. We had another document there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, but I just thought I would try not to interrupt the witness. But that problem has been there for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dzankovic a professional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- I believe our court deputy is checking with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought we'd got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dzankovic a professional security officer, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the war. That is the kind of problem that we had across the board with professional officers, and the same applies to the military security service. We had about 30 men. This fluctuated. We had about five or six men who had had professional experience with the service before the war, but this was a person with a university degree, with university education. He was an honourable man. And if we were convinced of someone's moral fibre, we would usually take them on and we would train them to perform their tasks. That was our only choice, really. Mr. Dzankovic had had a certain amount of experience during the induction period in performing operative tasks about town, clarifying issues that had to do with the work of the security service. Therefore, you can't say that he was an absolute layperson, but you can say that he was perfectly trained, a perfectly trained security officer. You certainly could claim that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what was your understanding as to what he was supposed to do in this inspection team?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they asked me to send him in, I didn't know what he was supposed to do, what his assignment would be about, except what I could tell based on the order indicating the competencies of the inspection team, the powers of the inspection team. Based on the order, this was a team that had to exercise control over certain issues of combat readiness, including the security detail. I was not in a position to make any specific assumptions. I simply didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What combat operations were these? What was your understanding?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever, none that I was aware of. I knew that he was to join a team headed by the Chief of Staff, one of my security service officers. What his specific assignments or obligations would be was something that I was in no position to assume at the time. As I have pointed out, by this time I had no idea about the Neretva 93 operation, its scope, or who would be involved. By this time. I'm talking about the time period when Dzankovic was to join the inspection team.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But you know now what he was sent for? Did you find out later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Hang on a moment. I object to that. My friend has to make that a specific question. If he's asking whether this witness has now come to a view -- well, in fact, the question -- I object to that question on a number of different grounds. He's already been asked why he selected Mr. Dzankovic and what he understood his role to be, and he's answered that question. Now, if it's being asked, has somebody else told him that Dzankovic was selected for some other purpose, then that can be asked. But otherwise it's simply a question either asking for him to give a different answer to the one he's already given or it's meaningless, because the witness has answered this, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that the witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I want to show the witness P146, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's correctly described as D146.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, D146. It's -- it's the Defence version as attached by that note from CLSS, Your Honour. This is the famous August order. Would you please give the B/C/S version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just raise a matter here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, no, I know it is. But I just -- I'm not sure whether the practice is changing that the witness be given a -- a paper copy of each document. It's not a -- it's not a practice the Defence is going to be able to comply with because we are operating within e-court and we are just simply -- in general, we're loading our documents up. It's probably not a concern generally, but I just want to mention it now that I've noticed it because we want to know that we're looking at the same thing that the witness is looking at. Of course I'm sure that that's the case. But it's a hard copy, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, with the e-court system, I believe that all the parties, including the witness, should rely on the documents appearing on the screen, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And in some occasions, maybe the witness is not in -- has a very good eyesight, you know, to stick to the screen all the day or, for some other reasons, the hard copy is furnished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, may I indicate, with respect, I agree with what Your Honour says. And if the Prosecutor has that view about a particular witness and they want to see a hard copy, then if the Prosecutor assures us it's the same thing, we completely accept that and we're happy for it to happen. Perhaps for the future it would be best if the Prosecutor mentions that that's going to happen in advance. I can't see it being a problem, but I can imagine situations that might arise. So for that reason, I -- I don't object to Mr. Jasarevic having this paper copy if the Prosecutor tells me it's the same -- it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been -- I have been giving the B/C/S version to the witness all this time, and now we -- we have this objection. This is the B/C/S version. It's the same version as the paper copy. It's D146. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that we have some problem with the documents. What if we had a break now and we'll come back at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that famous document on our screen. You may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasarevic, I've just shown you this document, and I will ask you, first and foremost: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the command of the -- Main Staff command, by General Rasim, on the formation of an expert team in order to control tasks in the area of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was this where you sent Dzankovic to, to this particular inspection team, as is delineated in this particular order?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at where it says "The main tasks of the team are as follows..." Would you please read this line: "Review of the combat readiness of the commands and units in the field and control of combat operations." Mr. Jasarevic, in your opinion, what does this -- what is encompassed in this one line?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first task, the first item in the order, talks about evaluating the combat readiness. Combat readiness has its elements, and they need to be checked. These are six elements of combat readiness which are checked through the institution of an inspection, and here it says, the commands of the units specifically out in the field. The term "commanding" or "controlling combat activities" is mentioned. The last word or the last three words here, to me, as a person who is not a linguistic expert, are unclear; namely, we have -- we have a comma here, and after that there is the word "and" and then the word "command" is mentioned "of combat operations." I'm not an expert to be able to interpret the absolute meaning of this part of this sentence, what it implies. Is it to control the command of these units or to command the combat activities of these units? This is a dilemma that I really don't know how to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How would you interpret the comma after "na terenu" and before "rukovodjenje," which is "in the field" in English, and a comma after this "and control"?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I responded already. I'm not a linguistic expert and I would not like to go into the interpretation of that. As a superior officer, as an officer, I know of another principle, and that is that orders to the armed forces, including our army, had to be issued in a clear way, in an unambiguous way. I would not like to go into the linguistic interpretations. A task would have to be clear to the soldiers, unambiguous. This is a principle that I would observe.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What authority would you think this particular order gave Sefer Halilovic in respect of combat operations, as you look at this order?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these tasks under item 1, except for this one, this part that we talked about, the last two words in the first item, everything else besides that is clear and I have no dilemmas about that. Point 2 is also clear, about which security officers are part of the inspection team. However, Your Honours, item 3 has a section introducing the obligation to the Chief of Staff that, in his orders, he can resolve the problems that crop up. This item 3 is much clearer than the one that we already commented upon, under 1, the first task, task number 1. From item 3, in the way that I interpret this order, the Chief of Staff has the right, under the orders of the staff commander and in accordance with his authorities out in the field, can resolve the problems that crop up, by his orders. However, Your Honours, I have already said that this sentence is much clearer than the first one, but for me, as an officer, there is still a minor dilemma. The words "in accordance with his authority" is mentioned. This is not quite clear to me what kind of authority is meant, the authorities arising from this order or those which the gentleman in question, Sefer Halilovic, as the Chief of Staff, has according to his post or function. This is a dilemma that I have not been able to resolve so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So do you know who was the commander of this military operation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the most complex of questions, to which I have never been able to find an answer. I actually don't know who was the commander of this operation because I never saw the order which would say who the commander of the Neretva 93 operation was. I am absolutely aware, as a superior officer, that for combat operations certain clear documents are required: First of all, an organisational order establishing the tasks, the time, the place, the composition, the command staff, the place where the operation is carried out, the participants, units, and so on are stated. Based on such an order, the situation is assessed. A little while earlier I expressed it in a more general way, that it would have been a good thing had I taken part in the evaluation of the situation. This evaluation would need to contain four crucial elements: the enemy force, the enemy strength evaluation, the assessment of one's own strength, the assessment of the terrain, and then the assessment of time as a factor of space, and also assessment of the weather. Then you would need an order for combat activities or a directive, if it comes from the Main Staff or the General Staff. And this order would imply participation in the drafting of such an order and helping the commander to reach such a decision. This is a process of work which is also prescribed under the rules. There can be no improvising in this procedure. Once the process of decision-making is completed - and this is what I have been talking about - this can also be done in a summary way, but the main principles in this process cannot be skipped. After such an order or a decision is reached -- no, excuse me, directive is drafted, then the combat documents are drafted, and then all of that has to be presented in detail. And it's quite a thick file, including the map of operations and other documents. I give you such a detailed explanation in order to explain why I wasn't ware of who the commander was of Neretva 93. What I have stated quite briefly here, because of all of those reasons, if all of this had been done, then it would have been quite clear who was the commander, which activities needed to be carried out, and how and in what way they would need to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But Dzankovic is your security officer which you allocated to Sefer Halilovic, which you said earlier on in your evidence, and you actually wrote that order that we saw. It was for this operation, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. My friend has to stop. Would Your Honours care to look at that proposition, argumentative in form and contrary to the evidence actually already given, and then consider what is being done by the learned Prosecutor here. And, frankly, disappointed by the answer, she's now trying to get another one. Now, that cannot be a proper question. And it's not just a question of form that I'm objecting to here, it's one of substance. Everyone in the court can see what the Prosecutor was hoping for, and -- well, I'm about to make a speech and I've already started. I'll stop. I'm sorry. I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I believe that Dzankovic is the security officer, you know, in this -- in the witness's unit, and that he was assigned to be a member of that inspection team --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the previous order, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Correct. Your Honour, if you look at the last line of the -- of the question, you'll see what the difficulty is: "It was for this operation, was it not"? Now, that's what -- that's where the problem lies in the question. The witness has said the contrary of that already. He assigned Dzankovic, and the evidence is quite plain, to be the security officer to Sefer Halilovic for the inspection team, as the order says, as he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the word "operation" is not quite clear, you know, what it means. Does it mean a military operation or does it mean the inspection team? You know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to say that the witness was shown a document where he allocates Dzankovic to the team commanded by Sefer Halilovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's not -- no disputes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- for the security administration, and that's what I was referring to in his previous testimony, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there's no disputes on that. But the question is about operation. What do you mean by "operation" by asking this question? So I ask you to put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you just saw this document, Mr. Jasarevic, which you have still before you, nominating Sefer Halilovic for a -- to control combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It's in the document, Your Honour. The witness has talked about it, before counsel gets to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is that correct? "Na teruna rukovodjenje," that one.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I explained quite clearly the first item under paragraph 1 of this order, and you can see from the first sentence in item 1 that this body, this team, where it states, "should coordinate the work and tasks in the areas of responsibility," and then later it says, "review the combat readiness of the commands and units in the field and control of combat operations," and then this is the linguistic problem that I was explaining. I don't see that Mr. Sefer Halilovic is the commander of the operation. If you permit me, since here the word "operation" is used, I would like to also express my opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you may certainly express your opinion, but can we just get back to my question and I'll give you an opportunity to express that opinion that you had. Was Dzankovic -- did you give him to Sefer Halilovic for this particular tasking, can I call it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allocated Mr. Dzankovic to be in the inspection team headed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you wanted to express an opinion. Would you now do that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "operation," the conduct of armed combat in our military is called "borba," fighting at the lowest level; then combat at a higher level, where more units, more force is used. In this case, it's a more extensive, more complex combat task or combat activity. Under this term, "Neretva 93", "Operation Neretva 93," "Neretva 93" is in quotation marks, it's a quote, in the way that this is the secret name for this operation. The usual practice - and this had to happen - is that all the documents that are formed in the part that I spoke about, that I spoke about a little bit briefly, about the estimate in -- that go in the decision-making and the drafting of the documents, each of those pieces of paper, each of those documents in the upper right-hand corner should have the kind of confidentiality level, the type of secret, and then underneath it should have the secret name, "Neretva 93," in quotation marks, and then underneath that, as 3 and 4, is the place where the copy, the number of the copy is stated. I never received such a paper from out in the ground with that particular title on the document, and that is why I cannot connect this or link this document with the Neretva 93 operation in -- not in a military, theoretical sense, or in the practical sense, in view of the distance of my position, and I was not able to de facto join this operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you did not see any of such documents, if they indeed existed. You don't know anything about them. That's your evidence, isn't it? You just simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's what he said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: My friend may cross-examine me if the Court permits her to, but she's not to cross-examine the witness, and I object to her doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution just asked confirmation from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If that's what the Prosecution is doing, Your Honour, well, Your Honour has ruled on it. I've made my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, it is your evidence - and I'm summing up what you've just been saying - is that if indeed any documents existed, you have no sight of them and you don't know anything about them. Is that your evidence by way of confirmation? It would be a yes or no answer, Mr. Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, no, no, no, no, no. Mr. Jasarevic can give his answer, without being told whether it has to be a yes or no by counsel in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this courtroom, I believe, first of all, the witness has to answer yes or no. That will save us a lot of time. If the witness feels the need to give an explanation, he's allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would that be a yes or no, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot respond to this question with a yes or no. The answer would be no, if it's connected to the secret name of Neretva 93 and that I never had any documents with such a name on it. However, I could respond with a yes if we're speaking about receiving certain information from out in the field. I received two pieces of information from Namik Dzankovic when he was out in the field, one piece of information from the security chief of the 6th Corps, and also one piece of information from the chief out at the Jablanica station, which were connected to the events out in the field. However, I am not familiar with the Neretva 93 operation as a military operation from which or in which I could say that I knew who the command was, the commander, and all the other elements that I mentioned as being part of a operation of that type.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what happened in the field I'll be coming to in a minute. But before I come to that, I wanted to just confirm that you had not seen any documents in respect of Operation Neretva 93. It's just -- this is what you had said earlier on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer with a yes to such a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Now, did you give Dzankovic his duties before he went to the command of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I said that Dzankovic was already out in the field and that -- and even if he had gone out as part of the team, I couldn't have issued any to him because I didn't know any orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So let's go to the field now, Mr. Jasarevic. What did you hear in the field, if anything, from Dzankovic? Did you hear anything in the field?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard from the field?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, here also I have to be more thorough. I received a report from the field from Dzankovic quite late, quite late. Before that, I received information from someone, probably via telephone, that a crime had occurred against the civilian Croat population in some Croat village in the Neretva River Valley. For a long time I couldn't remember who gave me this information. I assume that this came from Minister Alispahic. I assume so, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. Having found out about it - and this was probably on the 11th of September, in the afternoon or in the evening hours - I think that it was probably in the evening because I wrote some kind of guidelines to the chief of security of the 6th Corps. I usually didn't write these directions, I usually asked the drafter to put his initials on the left side and the person who types the document to put his initials on the right side. So by those criteria, I drafted such a document. And I -- I told or informed the security chief of the 6th Corps that there had been a crime in some Croat village against Croat civilians in the area of responsibility. I need to make a digression here from my main point because, based on this, you can tell that I didn't know much or anything about the Neretva 93 operation, the extent of the operation, the location, the command, and so on. According to my understanding, I sent two quite important tasks to the security chief of the 6th Corps: The first one was to check the information; and the second task was for him to propose to his commander the actions as you -- that you can see are mentioned in that document. That was my reaction in relation to what had happened. Later I will find out about the events in the village of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you ran ahead of me. I will be showing you some of these documents, and perhaps from there you can -- we can continue with your testimony. May I show you, please, 63 -- 63 is the 66 [sic] ter number, 02131910, MFI214. Can you tell us about this document, please. First of all, who is it from and who is it to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is from the military security service of the 6th Corps. It's sent to the security administration. And you can see the "to" and my initials. It was sent by the security chief of the 6th Corps, Mr. Nermin Eminovic. This document did pass through my hands, and this is my handwriting at the top of page 1 of the document. It's my reaction to the document. And, as you can see in the lower left-hand corner, the document was received on the 15th of September. It was drafted the day before, on the 14th of September, and this is my reaction. And you can see it here in "re your notification." It's a response to the document I sent on the 12th. As I said earlier, I apologise for going ahead of you. I was pulled forward by the time of the event because the -- what I said about Dzankovic will follow after this. This particular response came a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what is it talking about, this document? What is the substance?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who produced this document says that the commander of the military police battalion of the 6th Corps was out on the ground in order to give a hand to the military police company and the service detachment of the military police stationed at Jablanica. I'm just trying to go quickly through it. That he found out about what had happened over there. I immediately called this thing a crime. He also says that he couldn't get there pursuant to my request. All these are my reactions. Where you see things underlined, circled, exclamation marks, written by hand, these are by me. I was particularly confused by the fact that he referred to IKM, forward command post, and he continues to use this term. I used the term sometimes too when expressing my opinion. I was prompted by his use of term. He claims that everything was under control, but he places this in quotation marks himself. He says that the forward command post is holding everything under control. He also points out that this is a dangerous area to visit, again in quotation marks -- this is a quote based on what he said. Interesting, also, is the last sentence, which I underlined. He says that he has been consulted by Namik Dzankovic from the security administration. He says he was told or ordered, something along these lines, that because of an action that was already in the pipeline, nothing should be done about it for the time being. Purportedly, this is an order that was issued by Mr. Vehbija Karic, who had been a colonel before the war and who was a member of this inspection team. If you look at my reactions in relation to this document, there were a lot of things that needed clarifying. I tasked my immediate subordinate, Vahid Bogunic with this. I gave him these assignments. I'm not sure if I should comment on these too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What assignments did you give?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first assignment I gave him was to link this up with our communications so that we may know at all times the whereabouts of all those involved. It's a purely technical issue. The other assignment being very much a hands-on assignment, reaching the 6th Corps through Namik Dzankovic. I didn't know Mr. Dzankovic's whereabouts at the time; therefore, we should establish communication through the 6th Corps. Again, I'm pointing out that the problem of communications under those conditions was an extremely complex one. I also said that Dzankovic should inform us as soon as possible whose units were the units that killed over 20 civilians in Grabovica, who their commander was. You can see this initial attempt on my part to request information and to put together some sort of a picture of what exactly had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'd now like to show you another document, 62 on our 65 ter list, MFI215, 00587898.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is indeed the document I said earlier where I'm giving the Defence copy because of his markings on it, which I have already spoken to Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just want to ensure that Mr. Halilovic has the document in front of him which the Prosecutor is putting in front of the witness as well so that everyone is looking at the same thing. I think we'll get the English translation, but the Prosecutor wants to draw the witness's attention, I think, to some markings on the page, which she's entitled to do. But I just want to make sure that Mr. Halilovic has got -- has that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a document that the Defence would -- probably would put to this witness in any event, so we've got no difficulty with it being done. Right now I just want Mr. Halilovic to have a copy of -- of what he's being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could put that via Sanction, the document with the etchings of the witness on the document in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's put that document to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Is it available to the accused now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, could you look at this particular document and tell us about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's supposed to be an attachment, which is not there. There was an attachment that came with this document, an official note by the deputy chief of the Jablanica Public Security Station, Mr. Salihamidzic. At the end of the document which we have in front of us, in the lower left corner, it is clearly stated: "Attachment, official note." There's a stamp and a date at the bottom of the document showing when the document came in, when I received it. This is important because you can see how much time had elapsed before the document reached me, and this clearly illustrates the problem of communications at the time, prior to which I can say that this is a report that I received from Namik Dzankovic, who was out on the ground. The report --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what is this report? If you could tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- speaks --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- what the report is about and who is it from? Let's start with the beginning. What is it? Where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report came from Namik Dzankovic, a member of inspection team of the Supreme Command Staff. It's easy to notice, if you look at the heading -- again, it says "Forward Command Post." It was sent by Dzankovic, a member of the inspection team, and it speaks about a crime that occurred in the village of Grabovica against the local civilian Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it's to you personally, is it not? It's written up there: "Forwarded to" ...

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's addressed to the administration, and then I would usually receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What date did you get this particular document? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 20th. It should be in the attachment. I requested that an attachment be made, and I think there it is stated clearly the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did you request to be done? You say you have some of your own comments. Could you tell us the comments which appear on the -- on this document, your reaction to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm talking about Vahid Bogunic, who was then my deputy in the security administration. I gave him two assignments: Firstly, to inform the chief of security of the 1st Corps, because the units mentioned in Mr. Dzankovic's report belonged to the 1st Corps. Secondly, I ordered him to consult a legal expert and to come up with some measures to be taken. When I talked about the security structure in the 1st Corps yesterday, there was a legal expert there who acted as my assistant and who advised me on steps to be taken. This was very important for me at the time. Thirdly, on the right-hand side, where it says "analytical" and then "SI" with a dot, that means that they should draft a special report. Again, this is a much-discussed document that was sent to the five or six leading positions in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was this done?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Assignment number 2, or rather, item 2, in relation to this, there was a document that was sent back to Namik Dzankovic through the 6th Corps. This document contained certain tasks that Dzankovic was to organise and carry out. Two of the five assignments were in relation to the Jablanica Public Security Station. We were fully aware at the time, both my legal advisor, Goran Radovic, who happens to be alive and well, working as a municipal judge in Sarajevo, who is the author of this document, which I signed and which was sent to Dzankovic, who was out on the ground. As I was saying, we were fully aware that the task we faced was a complex one and that much time had elapsed. By this time, it was the 20th of September and we realised that Dzankovic couldn't handle this on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it to handle it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite definitely the commander of the operation either had to order that the problem be dealt with or create the necessary conditions, if he had the power to do this, to have this problem dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've answered that. I don't know who the commander of this operation was. It may strike you as unusual, but it's just the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, when you got this document which talked about crimes done, committed, between the night of the 8th and the 9th September - and I'm reading from the document - "Rifle shots were heard in the village which went on almost the whole night. In the morning, 9th September, news spread that the civilian population, that Croats had been massacred by BH army members from Sarajevo. Jablanica police station chief Emin Zebic, having been informed by two female Muslim refugees, who confirmed that several murders had been committed on the right bank of the Neretva, but he did not know the scope of the crime, nor who the perpetrators were," et cetera, et cetera. Basically it gives some horrific information; you would agree? Who was responsible for investigating this, according to you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to a later interpretation from people who were on the ground, the crime took place in the zone of operations during the Neretva 93 operation. There were military police and state bodies in the area. The highest-ranking officer was Mr. Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Somewhere in the area, I'm not sure about the specific whereabouts, the other military authorities in the area were the commanders of the 4th and 6th Corps - somewhere in the area, or in the broader area of the Neretva River Valley. These are three very powerful positions in the army. At the time, the Minister of the Interior was also present in the area as well as another minister, Mr. Mahmut Cehajic, another government minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is authority number 5 or 6. Mr. Cebo, who was the president of the War Presidency of three different municipalities, was also a highly-positioned person in the area, in the respective areas of Jablanica and Konjic. I can't quite put my finger on the person's name whom I don't know as operations commander, which means that I can't say that this or that person should have ordered anything, but it was absolutely impossible, bearing in mind the peculiar nature of the unit mentioned here as having committed the crime; namely, Ramiz Delalic, Celo's unit. If you look at this report, what clearly transpires - and we've looked at Eminovic's report a while ago - is that you can't have a proper professional inspection, which means that the only thing that could have been used to resolve the situation was power and authority, enforce an inspection. I must point out that in terms of the units that were present in the area, there was the military police battalion of the 6th Corps, the military police battalion of the 4th Corps. There was a civil police station in Jablanica, another one in Konjic, a detachment of the state security in Konjic. Bearing all these factors in mind, one realises that there were quite powerful figures in the area who, in my opinion at least, would have been responsible for carrying out an inspection and enforcing some sort of a solution. The first thing that had to be done was to arrest the perpetrators, and then you can take it further from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who were -- who would be the persons who would arrest the perpetrators? Who would those be?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the nature of those units, as well as the permanent threat which can easily be identified based on these reports, they simply did not allow civilian or military police into the area. I believe there is a hint in one of these documents by someone that this was in fact the case. Furthermore, there seems to be permanent hints in these reports that if an inspection was to be carried out, these would seriously prejudice and threaten any future combat operations. Based on these documents, you can see that the commander of the military police company from Jablanica went there together with the deputy chief of the Jablanica Public Security Station. It's in the attachment for you to see, Dzankovic's report that I referred to, the official note signed by Salih Amidzic, I really can't be sure. He speaks about precisely the same problem as Dzankovic. But if you look at this, you can see what a complex situation there was over there in the area. What it would have taken is a huge physical force to carry out an inspection like that, and only the operations commander would have had the authority to order something like that. This would have led to further consequences. I believe there would have been further casualties if this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At page 3 of this document, it says - if you'd look at page 3; it's the last page, although I don't know what page it is in yours, the last page - "Sefer Halilovic, who has disassociated himself from the crime, has ordered me personally to work with other military security service members and MUP officials to collect as much information as possible about the infamous event." What is your understanding of this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The description of the assignment as set out in this document has a certain value based on which one could conclude that Mr. Sefer Halilovic did react after all, that he gave Dzankovic an assignment to do something. However, Your Honours, I must point out that this was absolutely unrealistic from a purely professional point of view, and if we consider the objective circumstances surrounding these circumstances, then this objective situation is something that was described in all these documents that came in from the field. You have the same term recurring all throughout: Danger, danger, danger; threats, threats made by this man and by that man, over here and over there. It would have been extremely adventurous, even for someone much more qualified than Dzankovic, to take up these demanding assignments, professionally demanding assignments, to come to grips with these demanding assignments. It would have been unrealistic to expect Dzankovic on his own to deal with these. It's as if ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Whose superior was Dzankovic -- sorry, who was Dzankovic's superior?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzankovic's superior throughout this time, while the inspection team was still in existence, was certainly Mr. Sefer Halilovic. This was his team to all practical intents and purposes, as well as in theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So why was it that Mr. Dzankovic was the one who had to send you this report?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked yesterday about the assignments of the military security service. I said that there was vertical reporting to the service wherever its individual members were, at least as far as intelligence work was concerned, intelligence-related issued, as well as counter-intelligence-related issues. It reports on complex crimes. I think that's line 3 or line 2 of item 5, which speaks about war crimes. I commented yesterday that it speaks about crimes committed by the aggressor against us, but I believe the reverse is also true; a war crime is always a war crime, no matter who the perpetrator is. I believe Dzankovic's interpretation was quite correct in that sense. I'm not sure if I can remember this correctly, but I believe I read somewhere - and I can't be certain - that such an assignment was also given to him by Mr. Halilovic; namely, to inform the administration. I believe I found this somewhere, but I can't be positive about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I'll go back to that section I just read out to you. And if you would answer the question relating to Sefer Halilovic here, please, who says he has "disassociated himself from the crime." Why would he do something like that? What is your reading of that? Was he in charge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Namik Dzankovic's superior. Namik was a member of his team. To be quite honest, from a purely professional and linguistic point of view, this report is a little clumsy, to say the least, which makes it difficult to interpret. I'm not sure what Dzankovic meant, even less what Sefer meant, by ordering this sort of assignment or dissociating himself, as you said, from the crime. I believe that the author of this document, Dzankovic, probably used the term "disassociated himself from the crime," in a very conditional sense, meaning that he did not approve. The intention was to distance himself from what was done. But this, again, is a problem of interpretation and style more than anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, did you know the troops which were to be used and who were billeted in Grabovica who committed these crimes at the time -- before you saw this report? Did you know which troops were in the area in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. I didn't go down there. I was the security chief of the General Staff. So to know a soldier in a given brigade is not quite realistic. I knew Mr. Ramiz Delalic. And as far as his soldiers are concerned, I knew Mr. Adnan Solakovic, who happened to be there and is mentioned in some reports from the field, and also these more superior officers with whom I was in communication. But I didn't know any of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what -- would it have been Dzankovic's duty to do a security assessment before billeting these soldiers, since it wasn't yours?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not Dzankovic's duty because Dzankovic was not in the command. He wasn't an organ of the command, he was an organ of the inspection team. Had there been a command there, which is more numerous, which has its organs for all the elements -- as I spoke earlier about the assessment of the situation and the drafting of the combat documents, primarily the combat orders and so on, in that case the security organs, according to that scheme, would carry out an assessment of the situation. When we're talking about this, it is precisely one of the key mistakes that this assessment wasn't carried out, or I don't know about it being carried out, because when one estimates the strength of one's own forces and the terrain, a security officer would never propose that a unit -- or the unit of Ramiz Delalic, Celo, be billeted in the region, in the waiting area, which would be a location to the rear of the combat area, so to the waiting area, to some Croat village, when they are about to embark on -- into battle with Croats, some of whom are from that village. If, for objective reasons, in view of the time and the conditions, the weather conditions, that unit had to be billeted there, then it would not only be the task of the security officer but of other competent officers from the command to act in this manner; i.e., either to evacuate the civilian population from the village or to have this accommodation, which is called "bivak," the camp, in a waiting area where the soldiers would be billeted, provided with organs or somebody who would protect or secure that population to make sure that there was order there. I don't want to prejudice in any way the things that happened, but an evaluation implies the securing of law and order. So in such cases, to bring in a unit from outside, from some other composition, it has to be resubordinated to somebody. This is a well-known concept in command and control. So through the institution of resubordination, all of these instruments are secured - billeting, conditions of law, order, work, discipline, and so on. And if you would like, I could broaden my answer by the following: Any superior officer, the commander of a squad, a platoon, and then the commander of a company, as the highest ranking in this respect, would be responsible for the conditions, accommodation, discipline, and everything else which graces a disciplined soldier in such conditions. What I am trying to say is that these soldiers should not have been just left to their own devices like that. I noticed one detail from this document and its attachment, where it says that the units were brought on the 8th and the 9th in the afternoon, and already in the evening they started with shooting and exhibiting conduct that was very far from model conduct of a soldier. So the question I am asking myself is: Where are these superior units or the other authority's soldiers who are trained, who are intelligent, in order to stop this from going on?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you're not aware whether such a security assessment was actually carried out for this -- this billeting.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is precisely why I gave such a broad commentary, because I didn't know about it. If this had taken place, then that is quite a different question. Then the question would be why it wasn't carried out properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the time, I would like to refresh this witness's memory, with the -- with the Court's permission, and I would do that tomorrow. If that would be something -- a course of action I would be entitled to take, with your leave. I would like to bring in some of the relevant extracts from the statements and I would like to refresh this witness's memory on certain aspects of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I know how long do you still need to finish your direct examination to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't have very much longer. I have about four documents, which shouldn't take time. It will be purely putting them into evidence. I'm not going to take very long on them. Other than that, I would like to just refresh the witness's testimony on certain aspects, with the leave of the Court, of course. And that would take an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What do you mean by "refresh"?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, to show him his statements, some of the statements he's made, previous statements, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe we could stop here at this moment and we'll meet tomorrow afternoon. But anyway, we have spent a very long time here with the testimony. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let there be no doubt that there'll be a controversy tomorrow if there's any attempt made to refresh the witness's memory from those statements. So I won't argue it now. I'll just tell you that that controversy is coming if my friend attempts to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that depends how to do it, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the refreshment could be used in a way of questions and answers. I think there is no need to show the previous statements to this witness at all. It depends, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I agree. I just make it clear -- we'll await -- we'll await events.

utterances.text: Yes. Well, I believe that we have to stop here.
